catalog_quote: Le baoulé est une langue à tons, avec comme particularité notable un système particulièrement complexe de règles de combinatoire tonale selon lesquelles la réalisation du ton porté par une syllabe est influencée par les tons des syllabes adjacentes. Le système tonal du baoulé oppose trois tons ponctuels (haut, moyen et bas) et deux tons modulés (montant et descendant). Les séries de mots suivantes illustrent la pertinence de ces distinctions tonales : ... bué ‘nez’ ... buě ‘morceau’ ... sá ‘main’ ... sǎ ‘gingembre’ ... sâ ‘affaire’ ... blā ‘femme’ ... blâ ‘puits’ ... sìn ‘dos’ ... sîn ‘feu’
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Baoulé (baou1238) is not in the catalog. The five Glottolog title hits reduce to three works: Ahoua 1996 (book, twice), Leben & Ahoua 1997 (Phonology, twice) and Gut/Urua/Adouakou/Gibbon 2002 (TAPS). Gut et al. 2002 was downloaded open and read: an Anyi/Ega/Ibibio speech-rhythm timing study, Baule absent, no word-stress statement (irrelevant). Leben & Ahoua 1997 is paywalled (DOI 10.1017/S0952675797003321, Crossref-verified); its abstract concerns tonal prosodic-word domains (downdrift, H-sequence upsweep) and says nothing about stress. Ahoua 1996 has no open copy (Köppe sells the PDF; not in Google Books; PUB/DNB Anubis-blocked); the JALL 21(1) 2000 review snippets (already held by the project) report that it argues Baule is a tone language and not an accent/pitch accent language as earlier work claimed, with rhythmic weak/strong tonal alternation in right-headed feet — this is the high-priority acquisition. Byproducts downloaded from the TAPS 2001 proceedings (Gibbon 2002 Baule finite-state tone model; Ahoua & Leben tonal-change abstract; Leben 'Tonal feet'; Anyanwu on stress in African languages; Tchagbale on Tem) contain no Baule stress statement. The only first-hand stress statement held by the project remains Dolezal 1958 pp. 182-183 ('Das Baule betont fast durchwegs auf der letzten Silbe', from the 2026-09-16 pass), a 1950s impressionistic claim of final stress with faded tone that all later specialist descriptions (Creissels & Kouadio 1977, Quaireau 1982, Leben & Ahoua 1997, Creissels 2025, and Ahoua 1996 via its reviewer) contradict; a catalog entry should code Baoulé as tonal without lexical stress and treat Dolezal as superseded.

new_statements.quote: Akzent: Das Baule besitzt, wie auch andere Sprachen der Tschi-Sprachgruppe, „Töne“, deren Funktion jedoch weitgehend verblaßt ist. An ihre Stelle scheint nach und nach der dynamische Akzent zu treten. Dynamischer Akzent: Das Baule betont fast durchwegs auf der letzten Silbe. Man kann daher annehmen, daß ein Wort, dessen Betonung nicht auf der letzten Silbe liegt, zusammengesetzt ist, wobei die betonte Silbe die Kompositionsfuge anzeigt. Fremdwörter bilden selbstverständlich eine Ausnahme. Solche sind jedoch außer den französischen Ausdrücken sehr selten.
new_statements.translation: Accent: Like other languages of the Twi group, Baule possesses 'tones', whose function has however largely faded. Dynamic (stress) accent seems gradually to be taking their place. Dynamic accent: Baule stresses almost throughout on the last syllable. One may therefore assume that a word whose stress does not lie on the last syllable is a compound, the stressed syllable marking the compound juncture. Loanwords are of course an exception; apart from French expressions, however, these are very rare.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress ('dynamischer Akzent') falls on the final syllable of the (simplex) word almost without exception; a non-final stress is diagnostic of a compound, the stressed syllable marking the end of the first member (i.e. each member keeps final stress); French loans are exempt. (The IAI African Abstracts summary renders this as 'Stress is normally on the final syllable.')
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds (stress on the last syllable of a non-final member marks the Kompositionsfuge); loanwords, essentially French expressions.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement from a 1958 Kurzgrammatik (condensed from Dolezal's 1949 Vienna dissertation) that treats Baule as an Anyi dialect and claims lexical tone is largely non-functional — a claim contradicted by all modern work (Creissels & Kouadio 1977, Ahoua 1996, Leben & Ahoua 1997, Creissels 2025: 3 level + 2 contour tones, robust minimal sets). Modern primary sources read here are tonal and silent on stress; Ahoua 1996 (seen only via the JALL 2000 review) explicitly argues Baule is a tone language and NOT an accent language, attributing the earlier 'accent' impression to neutralisation of tonal contrasts in isolation, while analysing Baule rhythm as right-headed tonal feet. Delafosse 1901 (data partly Baule) gives a weak accent, default penult, attracted to a final a/o. Text of Dolezal seen only in Google Books snippet view (two scans, identical) plus the IAI English abstract; full pages not seen.
new_statements.identity_note: Dolezal 1958 is a short grammar of 'Baule' treated as 'eine Mundart des Anyi' (per Gipper & Schwarz's bibliographic note); dialect/informant base not recoverable from snippets (it condenses her 1949 Vienna dissertation). Modern reference works describe specific parlers: Creissels & Kouadio 1977 = parler de la région de Toumodi; Timyan 1977 = Kode dialect; Bohoussou 2008 = Nanafwe; Leben & Ahoua = 'Standard Baule' + Kode. Delafosse 1901's 'agni' manual (already held by the project under anyi1245) was learned during two years' residence 'au Baoulé' (Toumodi) and Creissels & Kouadio 1977 / Koffi 2022 say part of its data is Baule, so its vowel-quality-conditioned penult/final 'accent' rules arguably also bear on baou1238. All sources concern the same glottocode baou1238; no separate glottocode for Kode/Nanafwe at language level.

new_statements.translation: Baule possesses, like other languages of the Tshi group, 'tones', whose function has however largely faded. Dynamic accent seems gradually to be taking their place. Dynamic accent: Baule stresses almost without exception the last syllable. One may therefore assume that a word whose stress does not fall on the last syllable is a compound, the stressed syllable marking the compound seam. Loanwords are of course an exception.
new_statements.citation: Dolezal, Emmi (1958). Baule, Sprache eines Negervolkes an der Elfenbeinküste. Die Sprache (Wien) 4: 178-197. [Not one of the five title-hit items

new_statements.reading: Dolezal 1958 claims fixed final word stress (with non-final stress diagnosing compounds) and a tone system 'largely faded'. This is the only first-hand stress-placement statement found for Baoulé, but it is an impressionistic 1950s sketch and is contradicted by every later specialist source: Creissels & Kouadio 1977, Quaireau 1982, Leben & Ahoua 1997, Gibbon 1987/2002 and Creissels 2025 describe Baule as a fully tonal language (3 level + 2 contour tones, downdrift, H-sequence upsweep) with no stress category, and Ahoua 1996 (per the JALL 2000 review, pp. 101-104) explicitly tests and rejects the earlier 'accent language' classification while positing rhythmic weak/strong tonal alternation in right-headed feet. Carteron 1972 p.19 ('on insiste généralement sur la dernière syllabe') describes French, not Baoulé, by way of contrast with Baoulé tone. Recommended coding: tonal / no lexical stress reported; Dolezal's final-stress claim should be recorded as superseded. Nothing read in the five works with stress in the title gives a stress-placement statement.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

sources.citation: Delafosse, Maurice. 1901 [1900]. Essai de manuel de la langue agni, parlée dans la moitié orientale de la Côte d'Ivoire. Paris: J. André. (Cinquième partie, I. Accent, pp. 115-116.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: 'Il y a en agni un accent, mais il ne se fait que faiblement sentir'; denies 'intonation musicale'; rules: accent generally on the penult; on the final if its vowel is a/o unless the penult is also a/o; in 3+ syllable words antepenult if penult vowel is e/u/i; monosyllables unaccented; prefix a- never accented; compounds keep each member's accent. Author learned the language 'après deux ans de résidence au Baoulé'; Creissels & Kouadio 1977 (per Koffi 2022) say he described Baule rather than Anyi.

sources.quote: "Like the other languages in this group, Baule has phonological Low and High tones, and a Low tone lowers the register of following High tones – the phenomenon widely referred to as downdrift. But Baule is distinguished ... in that, within specified domains, sequences of two or more High tones exhibit a rise in pitch over the sequence. In this paper we show that the occurrence of the rising pattern over High-tone sequences helps to make a clear distinction in Baule between the prosodic word and the morphological word"
sources.note: Peer-reviewed statement of Baule prosodic structure (prosodic word, tonal domains/feet); likely states whether any stress/accent exists and where foot heads fall.

It was found that in sequences of all L tones, there is a..."; p.104: "...classified Baule as a pitch-accent language and some of which had suggested that Baule might have lexical tone contrasts.
